MR. CHOQUETTE-CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning notice of motion No. 1 on page 17 of the order paper, and standing in the name of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell).
On May 15, 1967, as recorded on page 187 of Hansard, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) asked you to strike from the order paper notice of motion No. 36 standing in my name.
Whereupon you replied:
-There may be arguments in favour of the proposition advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and if he will allow me to do so I will take that point under consideration and in due course, because I do not think it is a matter of extreme urgency, render a decision as to whether it is in order to allow this type of motion to be on the order paper.
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member for Carleton seeks to do indirectly what I would do more directly, that is the member for Carleton wants the royal power of dissolution abolished and-I end my question of privilege here-as the motion of the member will be studied today, I maintain I am being discriminated against if his motion is considered in order, because you have given no ruling.
That is why I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Emard):
That notice of Motion No. 1, on the order paper of the house under the name of the member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) be deleted therefrom and be considered invalid until such time as the Speaker has given a ruling on notice of motion No. 36 under my own name.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHOQUETTE-CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:

I must make the same ruling in the case of the question of privilege raised by
the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Cho-quette) and suggest that he may raise, if he wishes, a point of order when the notice of motion in the name of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) is called.

subtopic: REQUIREMENT THAT HEALTH WARNING BE PRINTED ON CIGARETTE PACKAGES
REQUIREMENT THAT HEALTH WARNING BE PRINTED ON CIGARETTE PACKAGES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-119, to amend the Tobacco Restraint Act.

subtopic: REQUIREMENT THAT HEALTH WARNING BE PRINTED ON CIGARETTE PACKAGES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: REQUIREMENT THAT HEALTH WARNING BE PRINTED ON CIGARETTE PACKAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am introducing this bill in order to call to the attention of the government the report which the Department of National Health and Welfare published after a study which lasted 12 years and proved that there is a direct link between excessive cigarette smoking and the mortality rate due to chronic illnesses such as lung cancer, respiratory ailments and heart disease.
In order to warn smokers and the coming generation against that danger, it would be advisable for the government to limit advertising with regard to tobacco and force companies to print on their packages of cigarettes: Warning-Smoking may endanger your health.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Chairman, on Friday I had started talking about air transport in Canada. Without repeating, it is crucial to remember that today in Canada we suffer from poor air service. The Canadian air lines, and particularly Air Canada, grossly underestimated the future volume of air traffic. The service we have in this country can now be roundly criticized, and especially that service provided in the west.

May 29, 1967
Supply-Transport
The main policy objective of the government was to make sure that Air Canada had enough business to finance its operations; that is, to buy good airplanes and provide good service. The determination to strengthen Air Canada, which was the government's main objective, ought not to have been the end at which the policy was aimed. That end ought to have been the provision of adequate services across Canada.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I contend we must provide for more competition throughout the country. When Canadian Pacific Airlines were given certain rights to fly across Canada I felt it was a move in the right direction, but I believe we are still unduly restricting C.P.A. in its operations. I am sure many hon. members are not aware that when Air Canada is given the right to serve a centre it is given the option of choosing the number of flights it will put on, times of departure and so on. Canadian Pacific Airlines, on the other hand, is given only the right to serve a certain city with a certain flight at a certain time; it cannot make any changes without the approval of the Air Transport Board. This is a situation which must be radically changed if we are to have a better air service across Canada.
This whole question will become further complicated as larger aircraft are introduced in the years immediately ahead. Very soon these bigger airplanes will be in service and scheduling will become more difficult; complicated adjustments will need to be made. Next year Air Canada will be receiving numbers of the elongated DC-8's which I understand will hold about 190 passengers. Obviously fewer flights will be needed to handle an equal number of passengers. Very soon the jumbo jets and the large jet-prop airplanes will be coming into service; I believe some of the air lines are already ordering planes which will hold 450 passengers. If we leave provision for air service in Canada in the hands of Air Canada alone it is my belief we shall end up once again with insufficient facilities.
It seems to me that one of the big advantages of competition in the modern world is that those who have invested their money in a business and made a study of it in order to reap a profit are those who will be most willing to work hard, take risks and look into the future as far as possible in a desire to give service to the public. They do this knowing that if they fail they are not likely to make any money.

Up to the present time, as far as competition is concerned, Air Canada has not had much to worry about. An excellent air line has been built up, but very little service has been provided. Let us change the criteria and put service first. I would remind hon. members that when T.W.A. wanted to start an air bus service from Edmonton to Calgary, Air Canada objected on the ground that it would lessen the number of passengers usually carried by them from Calgary and result in lower revenue; they could not stand the financial loss.
The fact remains that this air bus service did provide a facility which Air Canada was not giving and did not wish to give. What happened was that the T.W.A. air bus created new business. Air Canada lost little Edmon-ton-Calgary traffic, but businessmen now enjoy a good service from the centre of Edmonton to Calgary-six flights each way every day-and this has not affected T.C.A., as it then was, in the manner predicted by that company.
Broader competition would not only create new business, it would mean better service to the public as the result of an improved response to the needs of the people. Moreover, I claim it would not cripple Air Canada financially. At the present time Air Canada is making a tremendous profit, yet we in the west cannot get the air service we need. We know from experience that if this responsibility is left to one government agency only, the needs of the public are not put first; the daring and the imagination which are necessary are not displayed.
I believe T.W.A. wishes to start an air bus service from Edmonton to the west coast. I know the people of Edmonton want better service both to the west coast and to eastern Canada. In my opinion C.P.A. should be willing to make Edmonton a stopping point on its trans-Canada route, and should be given the right to do so in order to provide a truly trans-Canadian service on its route from Vancouver to the east coast. Canada is big enough for it, and the business is there.
I referred a few moments ago to plans for the introduction of larger aircraft on most of our commercial routes. I hope the Department of Transport is aware that many of our existing facilities will be outdated when these extra large aircraft come into service. At present the DC-8 carrying 120 passengers is the largest plane that can be handled at all adequately, and even so the service is not always efficient. Next year we expect the DC-9 to be
May 29, 1967

introduced, and it will not be long before the air lines are using planes capable of discharging a trainload of passengers at one time.
I trust the department will respond to the difficulty which this will create, and that airport managements are in consultation with the air lines to prepare the necessary facilities and methods of handling which must be introduced if the new aircraft are to be feasible. Time is short. In another two or three years the super jets should be here.
When there are jet planes capable of flying from Edmonton to Toronto in a little more than three hours I cannot understand why it should be necessary for passengers to wait half an hour to get their baggage. To say the least it must be frustrating to the air lines, which have provided fast airplanes to get passengers more quickly to their destinations.
I suggest that the concept of transportation from office to office or home to home should replace the existing concept based on time spent between one airport and another. Passengers must be conveyed not from city to city but from their homes or offices to their destinations, and this involves the prompt handling of baggage and the solution of local traffic problems.
I hope the department is giving consideration to this aspect of air travel. We have not heard a word about it so far, and perhaps the minister can tell us whether there is any special study group within his department currently looking into these questions.
I hope too, the minister will tell us whether there is any possibility of further competition on these air routes. I point out that this centennial year is one in which our shortage of airplanes shows up most clearly because of the pressure of Expo in Montreal. It is virtually impossible to get reservations for Montreal unless one makes them many weeks in advance. This is precisely the impetus which private carriers need so they may begin operations with a chance of showing a profit large enough to justify heavy expenditures in the future. I hope a decision to increase the amount of competition will be made now. It makes sense to take this step right away rather than wait until a peak year has gone by. I hope the minister will give his approval to this suggestion when he comes to reply.

In any event, as this newspaper article states, if you are planning a business or pleasure trip via Air Canada do not start packing your flight bag too quickly.
Much of our railway passenger service has been discarded apparently because the service was not being utilized. A sufficient number of planes to handle air traffic is not available and it would seem there is some difficulty in obtaining aircraft. However, other air carriers have indicated that they can provide service, and I think now is the time to abolish the monopoly position enjoyed by Air Canada. Air Canada is now operating at a profit. I suggest it is not necessary for a crown corporation to make a profit and that service should be the first consideration. Perhaps there should be competitive rates, but this is the time for the government to give some consideration to the possibility of allowing competitive lines to operate in this field, particularly in bottleneck areas like Ottawa where one cannot always get transportation in or out. If Air Canada cannot handle the traffic, let someone who says they can enter the field and compete for the extra business. It has been established that Air Canada has as much traffic as it can handle at the present time. As suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, the entire service
Supply-Transport
should be thrown open to competition, not only the service in places like Ottawa and Edmonton.
The minister professes to believe in free enterprise. If that is so, now that this crown corporation, Air Canada, has been looked after and is operating at a profit, perhaps we should allow free enterprise to provide service. I am sure that such service would be the best and cheapest available. The minister should give this whole idea some consideration.
Before I resume my seat let me again say, regarding the specific case I have brought forward in respect of air service at Maple Creek, that the minister should make some commitment that the board will provide an answer why this application cannot be accepted rather than simply saying that there would be insufficient utilization. This application should be accepted and some assistance should be provided. Some aircraft are now flying into this area.
Let me give one example of why this service is necessary. The area served by the hospital is very large and a radiologist must go into the area weekly. Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief observations without unnecessarily taking up the time of the committee. Of course you know I never do. But I have always been interested in transportation, having as a boy started out travelling by

Indian canoe, then by horseback and by steamers. As a matter of fact, I saw the first car in British Columbia in 1914. I have seen our transportation system develop over a period of more than 60 years.

Recently I had a cutting from a newspaper sent to me which indicates their appreciation, and I think it is only fair to compliment the government when it does something which is satisfactory to the people involved. installations have been made to improve night landing procedures and to better indicate traffic flow patterns on the runways.

Let me now refer to a matter of great interest to the people of southeastern British Columbia. It was referred to by another hon. member during our consideration of these estimates last Friday. I refer to the agreement with the C.P.R. to haul coal from the Crowsnest over a Canadian route.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

Ottawa facing a five-way dilemma in the "coal war".
Why Ottawa so involved in proposed railway line.
Kootenay & Elk line our newest railway?
Planning 70-mile long line, costing $14 million, to haul Rockies coal-and foil C.P.R.

coal over the Canadian route and the continued employment of the people who will be directly affected.
I now come to a rather interesting subject having to do with some complaints of the rank and file in the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen in the Kootenays. These complaints do not come from their head office in Ottawa but from the workers on the railroad. They have taken up these matters with their regional officers and have not obtained any support from them in drawing their complaints to the attention of the Minister of Labour. I understand these questions are also receiving the attention of the Minister of Transport. Before going further I want to say that I know the hon. member for Kootenay East is very interested in these problems because I understand he had a meeting with the railroaders in Cranbrook on the very issue involved.
These are the complaints the railroad employees make at the present time. There is no patrol of the railway at night. I am speaking now of the Kettle Valley line which has on it some very dangerous spots. I have travelled over it a good many times and have seen a good portion of that road built during my lifetime in that part of the country. These people tell me there is no adequate safety equipment on the trains. The safety equipment, if it is to be used satisfactorily, should be placed at the head end and not at the rear end of a train possibly over half a mile long. There are no rest houses provided on the road. There is some dissatisfaction among the membership of the unions with respect to the directives issued as to statutory holidays. In this connection I have received some fairly strong letters from individual members of the unions. I know practically all these men, many of them senior conductors, younger brakemen and so on. I should say that I know practically all the crews that go out of Nelson east and west, except for those who have been employed only in the last year or two.
These people do not make complaints without consideration. In my opinion they are sound complaints which should receive the consideration of the Department of Transport, the Department of Labour and their own organizations in Ottawa. I have some of the letters here. I am not going to read them all. They gave me permission to use what would
Supply-Transport
be considered unparliamentary language with respect to these circumstances in bringing them to the attention of the house. But, Mr. Chairman, I would not think of doing that with a lady member so close to my rear.
I wish to quote a letter received from the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, British Columbia sub legislative board, R.R.l, Nelson,

Further to a letter addressed to you by R. A. Hyssop, trainman on the C.P.R. from Nelson, B.C. and dated May 5, 1967 relative to the lack of adequate first-aid equipment on C.P.R. freight trains in particular.
Mr. Hyssop's letter has the endorsation of Lodge No. 558, Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen in Nelson, B.C., and it is my opinion that his letter is self-explanatory. He has documented an instance of a mishap he was involved in during the evening of January 16 last on the C.P.R. lines adjacent to the westerly shores of Lake Kootenay, where I might reiterate there is no other form of transportation media other than the railway. The highway is across on the easterly shore of this large lake.
It will be of interest to note that a similar wreck happened in about the same area approximately a year to the day prior to this one listed: and at that time, Mr. J. C. Young, a C.P.R. engineer from Nelson was quite badly injured. Broken bones and so forth. On that occasion it took over seven hours to transport this man to Kootenay Lake General Hospital.
There are no adequate first aid facilities on either engines or cabooses except for a very small pocket-size kit which might be O.K. for a minor cut finger or something of that nature.
I have personal knowledge in this regard because I have been on the trains. If anyone understands what railroading is like along the shores of Kootenay Lake he will realize that the possibility of rock slides and incidents of that sort is much greater than it is in many other places. The letter continues:
At the time of the Young incident, I wrote our B.C. compensation board to enlist their aid in having proper and suitable equipment supplied. They replied that their jurisdiction fell short of requesting or ordering the C.P.R. to do anything of this nature. We had the sympathy of the board,

but inasmuch as their authority did not extend that far, we were stymied.
The matter of supplying stretchers on cabooses in freight service is on record in our many briefs written by our various legislative committees in our various railway brotherhoods. To date we do not have any.
I am reliably informed that there is a move on foot to bring this matter of safety under some kind of a joint federal and provincial co-operative structure whereby matters of this nature may be properly presented with the hope that pleas such as ours will be carefully considered and if necessary acted upon. This is a very kind reference to the hon. members to whom the letter is addressed.
-to further this matter will be greatly appreciated not only by those unfortunate enough to be injured in wrecks, but also by those of us who never know from day to day when a calamity might occur whereby the presence of some adequate first-aid equipment, particularly stretchers, is an absolute necessity.
Thanking you, one and all, and with very best personal regards and all good wishes for the future,
I remain

Fred H. Lowe,
Chairman,
Joint Legislative Committees, International Hailway Brotherhoods in B.C.

In that connection I suggest that every effort be made to get the company and the officials of the minister's department to explain the circumstances, because it has been my experience that when it can be proven to the persons affected that to do so and so is not economic, generally speaking they are willing to accept the situation and adjust themselves to it. to operate, and finally the railroaders just brushed them aside and said they would take rank and file action to get something done in this connection. There is nothing I enjoy more than fighting in a rebellion, within any movement and I am very pleased to bring these matters to the attention of the minister. I am a bit of a radical myself. I am sure that something will be done to correct this situation. I have been on that road many times; I have been in the engines and the cabooses. These men have every justification to complain about the situation that exists.
I have brought to the attention of the minister the fact that there is no patrol in front of the trains at night, and such patrols are particularly required. I suggest to the minister that it would be a good idea for the officials of his department to visit these municipalities, examine the circumstances and advise them on how to proceed to take advantage of the legislation that is now in effect. One or two municipalities have made that suggestion to me.
Some time ago the city of Nelson made some tentative arrangements with the minister's department with respect to transferring to the federal government the ownership of certain property it held at the Castlegar airport in return for a grant for the building of

i much smaller airport at Nelson, B.C. I have rot heard anything about that in recent nonths. When the minister speaks I wish he would tell the Committee-if he does not have ;ime now perhaps he could let me know by correspondence-what the situation is at the present time with respect to the transfer of this land by the city of Nelson to the Cas-tlegar airport committee with a view to get-;ing a grant for the improvement of the present very small airport at Nelson.

More and more small planes are coming in from various parts of the province end wanting to use small airports. Even in tny own district in the Arrow lakes it is proposed now to build a small airport. Because many of the people concerned do not lave much technical knowledge of what is required with respect to the site and location with relation to other surrounding circumstances, I suggest that the officials of the minister's department be prepared to give these smaller communities technical advice with respect to the location of small airports and their development and advice on how to proceed to obtain some assistance from the federal government in this connection. I suggest that the minister could well consider expanding the public relations branch of his department so that the communities, the farmers' organizations, chambers of commerce and unions are made aware of what the federal government intends to do in a certain area. I also made this suggestion in connection with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and I am very pleased that senior officials of the C.B.C. have visited Trail, Rossland and other small communities to discuss the local circumstances with the people concerned. As

a result these people know what the policy of the C.B.C. is with respect to matters relating to television, radio, relay stations and so on, and the officials understand better the reasons for which these people are seeking this or that. I do hope that suggestion will be given some consideration.
In conclusion I wish to speak about transportation research. I am all for it. We are living under changing circumstances. In my own short span of life, which I am hoping to prolong as long as possible, I have seen the development from very primitive forms of transportation to railways, highways, airways and so on. I think it is very necessary that research into transportation be undertaken in co-operation with the provincial governments, not necessarily into the technical side of transportation but so that the federal government will know what any provincial government has in mind with respect to the development of a certain industry, a certain resource, or possibly the development of the provinces highway policy. Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments to answer the questions raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I do not intend to deal with all the matters raised by him. However, first I should like to assure him that we do have a meeting of minds on quite a large number of matters, one specific difference being the question of socialism versus free enterprise. But in so far as our concern for our fellow man and the public generally is concerned we do agree on most matters.
It is true that I held a meeting with the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway in Cranbrook a week ago last Thursday to discuss specifically the question of safety on that section of the railway with which the hon. member and I myself are familiar-along the west bank of Kootenay lake where no other mode of transportation is available and where the slide area is extensive. Of course there is an unusually large amount of freight passing over that line. The reason is that practically all the freight shipments from west Kootenay

May 29, 1967
Supply-Transport
to the coast are baekhauled from Nelson to Cranbrook and up the Columbia valley to the main line.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Some time ago the Canadian Pacific Railway did remove the night patrol that had customarily patrolled that area several times during the hours when there are no section-men available on the track itself. There have been a number of accidents. The one to which the hon. member referred was a very serious accident and I am told that the injured lay for some five to seven hours before being transported to hospital. This is an intolerable situation and I have expressed my opinion to the Department of Labour, to the Board of Transport Commissioners and, of course, subsequently, to the Canadian Pacific Railway itself.
There is I think, some reason to believe that the officers of the union have done as much as they found possible. There is some measure of confusion at the moment about jurisdiction in respect of safety regulations on railways, that is, whether they come under the compensation board of the province or whether they are directly related to the Department of Transport. This matter is being clarified under our new Department of Labour safety and hygiene measure. I have arranged a meeting tomorrow with the legislative representative of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, at which time we will discuss the matter further and determine what action should be taken. I am sure the hon. member will realize that we consider this question to be a serious one and hope to have it cleared up in the near future.

Mr. Chairman, I will only take a few minutes of the time of the house to bring two points to the attention of the minister, that is the air service and the C.N.R. passenger service in the area which concerns me.
First of all, let me congratulate the minister for his patience in listening to us and for the way in which he accepts our requests and our complaints. He always has a smile on his lips and I wish his acceptance was initiated by the companies involved, that is the crown corporations which do not seem to pay as much attention to our remarks and to our appeals as the minister does.
I think the crown corporations have somewhat too much latitude and that the minister lacks some authority over these corporations,

because they do not want to fulfil their purpose of serving the public. In fact, if I understand the reason for creating these corporations, it is first and foremost to serve the public for, after all, the public is paying. Now, when we ask for a service, when we point out some weaknesses, they seem indifferent, they seem above these small details and these questions are put off or completely forgotten.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the crown corporations are showing a lack of social conscience and that they are neglecting their duty, and when they come here and ask us to pay their deficit which is often due to their own inefficiency, I feel that the minister should have the authority to make them think or to rebuke strongly those officials who are not only unable to balance their budget, but who cannot make profits like other companies, such as the Canadian Pacific, for instance, which shows profits every year. I believe that if the officials of the Canadian National were as skilled and serious, we could get an adequate service and not call upon the taxpayers every year to replenish those crown corporations.
Mr. Chairman, this was not the main part of my remarks, but I wanted to draw the attention of the minister on that situation.
Now, I would like to call his attention to the matter of air transportation of passengers in my area, that is Lac Saint-Jean and more precisely Roberval. I do not know whether the minister is aware that we have a very small airport in Roberval. He nods to indicate that he knows; I think that he has already landed at this airport.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It is not a big city airport but we value what we have and I think that something could be done about that airport. At the present time, it is an asphalt strip which has been used for several years already but not regularly since 1960, and even Nordair Lt6e which used it did not renew its contract last year.
On March 29, 1967, the newspaper L'Etoile du Lac published an article entitled "Nordair returns" after an interruption of almost four years in the passenger service. I am not talking about the commercial service, because it was possibly a little too profitable for Nordair, and that may have made it forget the passengers. Since its licence allowed the company to concentrate most of its business in Montreal, it followed in part the example of the C.N.R. in transferring everything to Montreal; all one can see now in the Roberval
May 29, 19G7

area are Nordair planes flying north without stopping in the county of Roberval.
This is what Roland G. Lefrangois, president of Nordair Ltd. wrote:
If the town of Roberval does not object, the Nordair Ltd. airline will re-establish its daily service between Roberval and Montreal. That is what the president of the company, Mr. Roland G. Lefrangois, has just announced in a letter to the airport committee of the Chamber of Commerce of the district.
Recalling that his company had provided such a service from 1956 to 1960, via Chibougamau, Quebec city, La Tuque and Chute des Passes, and that it had not proved very profitable precisely because small private companies like Nordair received no help from the governments in those areas.
-and had to be discontinued in 1960, Mr. Lefrangois explained that a new policy of the Department of Transport now made it possible to re-establish the service-
Further on, it is written:
After reminding that Nordair had all the facilities necessary for such a service in Roberval, Mr. Lefrangois observed that the undamaged part of the runway would be adequate for the planes which the company wanted to use.
Mr. Chairman, if we talk of sacrifice, I think the town of Roberval has done its share, since it had to pay over $300,000 to co-operate with the government and construct this runway.
As regards the present condition of the runway, it is easy to understand that an airstrip that has not been used every day, during four years, has deteriorated; in fact, it was somewhat damaged through bad weather, cold weather and frost and a complete sinking in of the strip is even to be feared. After so many sacrifices on the part of the company, the government and the town of Roberval, the government must not let that runway deteriorate any further.
Officials of the Department of Transport came to Roberval in March and promised to proceed with the necessary repairs in June or July. Last spring, the town of Roberval cleared up the airstrip by itself and took care of minor repairs, and we would like the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), to draw that to the attention of the commission and refresh its memory about it, so as to have that part of the runway reconditioned since, at present, there is about one third of it which is damaged.
I would also ask the minister to intervene with the commission for the granting of the
Supply-Transport
permit requested as soon as possible, in accordance with the new policy of the government concerning small airports, since that will permit the operation of an economic route for our area, considering that that is the only federal airport in the constituency of Roberval, at present. I think the minister must see to it that our area is served as fairly as the others.
We now have the undertaking of Nordair, in that connection, for November 1967, that is for the fall. But we feel we must have more adequate service sooner, because of Expo in Montreal and forthcoming industrial developments in the county of Roberval. I will point out to the minister that if Nordair does not hurry in applying for a permit, Quebecair seems very interested in giving us air service. In fact, in the newspaper I'Etoile du Lac of April 19, an article concerning Quebecair read as follows:
From usually reliable sources, we learned last night that the directors of Quebecair, amongst others, the vice-president of the airline, Mr. Fournier, will visit the area shortly to meet our businessmen and municipal leaders and discuss the possibility of re-establishing the daily air service between Montreal and Roberval, via La Tuque and Chibougamau.
Quebecair, a company administered by the Briant family of Rimouski, already uses the base at Bagotville, and, it seems that this French-Canadian firm would be willing to consider the expansion of its air service.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think we now have the choice between two companies and if the first one does not want to move faster, we certainly have a good opportunity with Quebecair. The minister should point that out to the commission, to its members, because it is a very important and vital matter for us. At present, that is the only airport we have, and when we want to make a quick trip, the service through Bagotville is not satisfactory because we have to drive 200 miles to reach the Lake St. John area.
We prefer the airline to the railroad since it is practically impossible to get adequate rail service. And that brings me to say a few words about our good old Canadian National. I see the minister laughing a little. He has good reason to do so because that old train is hobbling along wondering whether it will reach the end. It is faithful to its slogan: Let us keep our delays.
As I have to use that last means to cover the 500 miles or so to get to my work here, in Ottawa, I must tell you that I have sometimes the impression that the authorities have decided to make that line so hated by the passengers that they will themselves beg for its

May 29, 1967
Supply-Transport
abandonment. And we pay those men $75,000 a year to use the taxpayers' money in that manner.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
For instance, a roomette costs $9, meals included, but meals are not available because they are never served on that train. The cost is $9 all the same, and it takes 18, 19 or 20 hours to cover a distance o1 500 miles nonstop. Moreover, and the minister is perhaps aware of it, C.N.R. trains are prohibited from exceeding 30 miles per hour between Chambord and Dolbeau. Over 30 miles per hour, the train could become derailed.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, something could be done, but in spite of all our requests and of all our entreaties to C.N.R. authorities, we have failed to obtain any results. And I know from experience because I board that train every week. In winter, especially in extremely cold weather the situation is worse. On one trip, it is very hot, and on the next very cold. I have even had to get up at two in the morning to put on my winter clother in order to get to Chambord without freezing my feet, my hands and face on the train. And if we have heat, the situation is the same.
I have asked if it would not be possible to get a technician to control the equipment, but that is impossible. The last time I left Montreal, I saw the technician adjusting the temperature. I asked him: Do you think we will have a normal temperature this time? Each roomette is equipped with controls to set the temperature but the equipment is nothing more than a toy. In fact, you play with the gadgets and nothing happens. I asked the man in charge: Do you think we will be comfortable? He answered: It is warm now, but I do not know what will happen at the other end. He, of course stays in Montreal. Everything is concentrated in Montreal. You can imagine what fate awaits the passengers.
Last winter, I saw women with babies freezing on the train; there was no heat. At one point, I got up. I do not hold it against the train conductors, they do what they can, their utmost. What can they do when there is no heat, when the equipment is not working properly? Sometimes, tricks are played on them because they do not know. I could hear women in the other roomettes shouting: We are freezing, we are freezing. As I am getting to know the various train conductors, I asked the porter? What have you done' The steam was not going up; not only that, he had opened the cold air valve. Instead of getting at least a little warm air in the roomettes, we

were getting cold air. He had opened the wrong valve.
If, at least, we had someone who knew what to do on a long stretch like that, especially in winter when it is 40 below zero. It is a question of public service and protection. It is either cold or hot. And if they put on the heat, the same thing happens. The other day, every steam valve had been opened. There is no way to control anything. The windows could not be opened. At that time, we were dying of heat on the train. I asked the conductor if he could turn off the heat and he answered: The only thing I can do is open the doors at both ends; there is no other way to control it.
I am telling the minister that he is just the man to bring this to the attention of those who will not listen to us. It seems as if they did not want to. I do not know whether they lack goodwill, but they are unwilling to listen to us.
It was like this all winter; it was either too hot or too cold, but we never could obtain a normal temperature.
On other trains, for instance between Ottawa and Montreal, the temperature is normal. But when we get on our trains, it seems as if we were supplied with the oldest material, with anything that is unmanageable, so that when passengers arrive at Dolbeau, Normandin, Chambord or Roberval, they swear they will never be caught again, the C.N.R. will not catch them to return to Montreal.
That is why I was telling the minister that those companies must absolutely be forced to give the service, and if they do not, let them vacate the field for the Canadian Pacific for instance, or other companies. In addition, if the men are not serious enough to take care of people's health and welfare, let them be taken out of there. People can be replaced. At $75,000 per year, Mr. Chairman, you could have several men, and good men at that.
Mr. Chairman, those are the two points which I wanted to draw to the minister's attention. I know he will do what he can, but I believe he does not have, as of now, enough influence on those crown corporations which have become almost all-powerful, and I do hope that some day the government will give him more latitude to force those crown corporations back to reason. I think that completes my remarks on the point I wanted to raise. I would now like to deal with another. I received this morning a letter from Arvida about the telecommunications system. It
May 29, 1967



comes from a businessman who complains about the system aboard that train which does not operate directly in my region, since it is the train from Chambord to Chicoutimi. Here is what he says:
I would like to complain here about the quality of the service given us by the C.X.R.'s telecommunications service.
I apologize for raising this matter, Mr. Chairman. That letter comes from the riding of Lapointe and I quess the writer preferred to send it through me. I continue:
I think the present situation is intolerable in a region like ours and should be remedied as soon as possible.
On Friday night. May 19 last, after an urgent meeting, the executive of C.A.M.A., our association, sent to the out of town directors, through the C.N.R.'s telecommunications service, a rather important night letter. That message arrived in Chicoutimi at four minutes past eleven o'clock; the employees tried to reach me but, since I was not at home, they left the following message: Mr. Dostie has received a telegram; we close at
11.30 and we will call him back on Tuesday because no one works during the weekend. May 22 being a legal holiday, the telecommunications service was therefore closed during 80 consecutive hours.
I sincerely believe that this situation should not exist, that this decision was taken too hastily by the C.N.R., that they did not try hard enough to find a solution which would make it possible to keep the telecommunications service in operation at least 16 hours a day during a period of 365 consecutive days.
If the Chicoutimi system must be closed, telegrams should be routed through Quebec City or some other centre, and transmitted from there by telephone. If this procedure is too costly, further research should be made, but means should be found to keep the telecommunications system in operation 16 hours a day.
This is signed by a Mr. Clement Dostie, from Arvida. I think this letter should be mentioned here and brought to the attention of the C.N.R. people.
Now, I have received many complaints about this railway line. I have never mentioned this in public because it is a semi-public semi-private institution, but when nobody makes a move and everybody seems asleep, I think the time has come to bring the matter to the attention of the public at large.
The problem concerns a night porter on the Chambord-Chicoutimi run.

1 do not know if the minister has heard about it-who does his duty and is even over-zealous for he wakes women up at two and three in the morning to ask them for ten or fifteen minutes off. I wish to comment now on a continuing problem which arises in connection with the air terminals of this country. I am not an engineer but I wonder whether the time has not come to undertake a giant study of means by which passengers could be transported more quickly from terminals to downtown centres. Expo has shown us what can be done by using imaginative transport policies. During my stay in Ottawa one of the most hair-raising parts of that experience has been taking the air line bus along what I believe to be the Hunt Club road out of Ottawa to the terminal. It is certainly more hazardous than any jet flight I have undertaken, and the need for seat belts is even more evident. Could not journeys of this kind be made easier by the use of monorails, for example? I notice that Dr. Solandt had some most imaginative things to say the other day about planning in the next hundred years of Canada's history and I would think that high on the list of priorities should be the project I have mentioned.
My hon. friend from Edmonton-Strathcona talked about supersonic jets. I suspect that if he and I were to discuss this question our views would be opposed. I worry not so much about possible difficulties in embarking or disembarking as I do about noise and other interferences with daily life. I presume that the National Research Council or some of the minister's own officials are even now studying the effects of noise and other nuisances which will be caused by aircraft of this type.
To turn from supersonic jets to the National Harbours Board, may I say that for some time I have requested that arrangements be made in the port of Saint John for the offloading of feed grain. Though all the necessary facilities are there for the loading of grain in an efficient manner, it is interesting to note that there are no facilities whatever for offloading. What the port needs is a leg, I think it is called, before its full facilities can be used.
My concluding comment is even more parochial, though perhaps the concept is not. It is a request that the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works should work together very closely in connection with the provision of navigational aids and other amenities on our great waterways. I believe

"Commercial use" should be interpreted very widely, because in these days of shorter working weeks our citizens are much more readily able to acquire power boats and so on. I was unable to persuade the former government to adopt this view but I have not given up hope of converting the present administration. These waterways are a priceless asset. I know the minister and his department have co-operated in seeing that navigational aids are brought up to date in some cases, but time and again when I recommend certain changes or the provision of amenities along the Saint John river system I am asked: What is the commercial use?
If that means unloading logs for pulp and so on, there is very little commercial use. But within the last 12 months the river system and the people of New Brunswick played host, as it were, to the Cruising Club of America whose members arrived in $2 million worth of sailing boats and other craft. It would have been an unforgettable experience could those yachts have benefited from modern navigational aids and other amenities such as garbage disposal facilities, ice, oil, fuel and so on.
I hope that at some time when historians are poring over the remarks I am making today they will be able to celebrate a day when the great purpose of the river system will be to meet the needs of the man who seeks to revive his spirit by taking to the clean waters of the Saint John river, something which could be made easier and more pleasant if we really made the best of the wonderful inland water system which is part of Canada's heritage.

May 29, 1987

spoke of the need for better air service and recommended increased competition among air lines. I suggest to those hon. members that the question is not as simple as they would have us believe. The basic difficulty is the shortage of planes. If tomorrow, for example, the Air Transport Board were to say to Canadian Pacific Airlines, "You can have all the rights you want", the fact is they would have great difficulty in providing service. The shortage of aircraft today is critical. Because of the war in Viet Nam the production of military aircraft is being given priority in the United States. The shortage of aircraft is not confined to the two larger corporations. I should like to add this comment in that connection. Some reference has been made to the minister's own air line, the aircraft of the Department of Transport. There are three government air lines-Air Canada, Department of Transport aircraft and the aircraft of the Department of National Defence. In respect of aircraft of the Department of National Defence particularly, the policy has been that they do not carry people who normally should travel on commercial air lines. One can understand the reason for this. In the past the commercial air lines have complained. We find that when members of parliament are travelling to official conferences they are sometimes allowed to travel on government aircraft, but if their wives accompany them they must go by the commercial air lines. for many hours in Toronto. Only those who come from distant points in the country realize how critical the situation is. now it is doubtful that a tunnel or bridge could be completed before 1970 or 1971. I understand that the new airport in Vancouver will be in operation next year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to talk about airports, specifically municipally developed airports to which the government contributes under its program and, second, airports which are built under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport, which I believe are referred to loosely as national airports. Historically my riding has been a railroad transportation constituency. With the decline in railroading we have been attempting to broaden our economic base by developing the tourist trade. An increasing number of tourists are now coming into our area by air. We have been pressing the Department of Transport for airports, specifically for airports at Sioux Lookout, Red Lake, Dryden and Kenora. I should like to deal with each of these centres in order to illustrate what has been going on for some time.
In respect of the regional airport assistance program I notice under vote 40 that for the fiscal year 1966-67 the amount provided was $1,608,000 and that for 1967-68 it is being reduced to $1,386,700. This is a very valuable

program. I should like the minister to explain why the program is being cut back. I should like to see an increased appropriation for this program.
May I deal first of all with the situation at Sioux Lookout. I had a meeting there with the town council and chamber of commerce to deal with the airport situation. For four years now they have intermittently been making application to the Department of Transport to have their airport runways resurfaced and lengthened. After four years the answer they received was no. This was a bit of a blow to the people of Sioux Lookout because when TransAir of Winnipeg made an application to operate a flight from Winnipeg via Red Lake and Sioux Lookout to the lake-head and back again Sioux Lookout for the first time was going to be on an air line schedule. Unfortunately, the day before the flight was to be inaugurated the Department of Transport informed TransAir that it could not land at Sioux Lookout because the runway was too short. It was 2,800 feet and under the regulation it is necessary that it be 3,600 feet. Yet the DC-3 aircraft, which were to be used, are still landing at Sioux Lookout, although I must admit they are being used as cargo rather than passenger aircraft.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The point I want to make first of all is that the Department of Transport has been remarkably lax in taking such a long time to answer such a simple request. Second, the TransAir schedule had been known for some months before the service was to go into operation. Yet the day before it was to be inaugurated, permission to land there was denied. In any event, DC-3's are still landing there.
The third point is that even though the cost of extending the runway to 3,600 feet, to make it long enough for DC-3 passenger aircraft to land, would be high, about $300,000, I think the Department of Transport has taken the wrong approach. Even though the cost would be high, the fact is that with regularly scheduled flights landing there, there would be a certain amount of revenue to the Department of Transport which otherwise they will not receive. Unlike other airports, there would be a certain return to the Department of Transport as a result of the scheduled service that would be provided. I understand it would be a six-day service.
May 29, 1967



Another situation I wish to refer to exists at Red Lake. There has been an air connection between Red Lake and Winnipeg via TransAir for some time. Last year I was told that the Department of Transport was going to extend the runway and resurface it to a length of 5,000 feet. This plan was cancelled because the cost was apparently too high. This project was to be included again this year in the plans, but apparently it has again been cancelled. I do not know what the reason is for cancellation this time because I only heard about it from the local people yesterday. There does seem to be something suspicious about this situation in view of the fact this plan was supposed to be included in the estimates for two years but has been cancelled both times for no real or apparent reason.
Let me now deal with the situation which exists at Dryden. The people there have requested the development of an airport under the regional air development policy. I received a letter today from the chairman of the committee making the application to the department. The committee is bothered because of the small allotment of money in the estimates for the next year, approximately $1,300,000 for the whole of Canada.
The people of the area do not know how much chance they have of getting any money in order that they may proceed quickly with this project, and TransAir has promised them that if the project is proceeded with quickly Dryden will be included in the flight schedule between Winnipeg and the lakehead. I should like to see some other means of allotting this money worked out because the present system does not do much for northwestern Ontario. That area is included by the Department of Transport in the Winnipeg region. This means that before our needs are likely to be considered the needs of the province of Manitoba will be looked after by the department. Perhaps the minister would consider establishing a new region for eastern and northwestern Ontario in order that this area will not be considered after the province of Manitoba. There is some reason to believe that this is the situation at the present time.
The other airport I want to talk about is that at Kenora. It is also operated by the Department of Transport and there have been efforts to get the runway extended to 5,000 feet in order to service the business being generated in this area by the tourist industry. This is becoming increasingly important to the economy of Kenora as the income re-
Supply-Transport
ceived from the railway industry becomes less.
The cost of extending this runway would be quite high, but the people of Kenora are attempting to get a regional air line from the United States to provide a service there. This again would provide a certain amount of revenue to that airport. The cost of constructing airports in northwestern Ontario is very high, as the minister is likely aware, because of the terrain with which we must work. In view of the fact that this area has reached an all-time low so far as railway service is concerned, perhaps the minister ought to look at the situation from the point of view that while airport construction is expensive this is an investment in the future of the area. This area must be developed if it is to grow and survive.
The modern method of air travel is becoming increasingly more important, and I appeal to the minister to do something about the difficulties which result from the allotment of money under the regional airport assistance program. rates. I hope the minister will comment on this when he replies and tell us what will happen to freight rates when the complete implementation of this measure is brought about. It has been brought to the attention of these gentlemen that apparently Canadian National Railways plans to abandon trains Nos. 218 and 217 which operate between Stratford and Toronto. It is apparently planned to abandon these trains early in July this year in favour of highway transport. These gentlemen point out that the train takes three hours and a few minutes in its journey from Stratford to Toronto. It stops at Kitchener, Guelph and Brampton, picks up several cars of freight at each stop, and on the return trip it drops cars of freight at these places. Twenty five to 28 carloads of freight have been hauled per trip. On the return trips there are not as many freight cars but in both directions the trains carry piggyback trailers.
May 29, 1967

Apparently it has been proposed that this Canadian National freight service be turned over to highway transport entirely. These trains cover the distance in three hours and a few minutes each way and give very prompt service in picking up traffic en route. I believe that if this traffic is hauled by road it will only further clutter up the highways. It is really railway traffic in the first place and, as the two gentlemen who signed this letter so succinctly point out, if the trains are cancelled railway traffic will no longer be travelling on the rails where it belongs but on the highways. Mr. Chairman, I wish to place on the record what I and I think most citizens on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river in Laprairie county, along the length of the seaway channel from St. Lambert to Laprairie, the Cote Ste-Catherine locks and Caugh-nawaga, consider to be the basic responsibilities of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. In 1957 and 1958 when the St. Lawrence seaway was built along the south shore of the St. Lawrence river the citizens of this area were assured that the initial scars of construction would soon disappear. In its commitments to individuals arising out of land expropriation, the seaway authority has, not without some nudging, fulfilled its responsibility toward shoreline owners. I must say in fairness that in many cases it has actually brought shoreline properties to a better state than existed prior to the seaway construction. The seaway authority has also settled satisfactorily most of the differences which existed between it and the affected south shore and Laprairie county municipal bodies. Caughnawaga is one exception to this, but negotiations have been under way in earnest for the past two years in the latter case, after a long period when communications had broken down. I am hopeful that the Caughnawaga band can be adequately and fully paid for the expropriated band lands and rights without too much additional delay.
Having said this, let me add that the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority has failed in its commitment to the Canadian public, and more particularly in its obligations to the citizens of the south shore and Laprairie county, with regard to the portions of land which it expropriated and then kept. I refer specifically to the unfilled excavations and rubble piles left untouched since the last construction bulldozer left the site eight or nine years ago. In the city of Brossard these eyesores, which for years were hidden from all but the suffering local citizenry, are now exposed to millions of Expo visitors because a six-lane highways has been completed along the shoreline.

I am pleased that last autumn the seaway authority acceded to my request and hired a landscape architect to prepare plans for beautifying this portion of the seaway property. The landscaping needed may well be expensive, but it is clearly the responsibility of the seaway authority to see that such landspacing take place and that it be implemented without additional delay.
The seaway authority has been dragging its feet, hoping that higher tolls will provide it with additional funds for this purpose. The United States government has now rejected any increase in tolls and the seaway authority must now face up to its obligations. I hope the minister will lend his support to an effort by the seaway authority to eliminate this year the affronts to nature which the authority created nine or ten years ago at Brossard and at Caughnawaga at the approaches to the Mercier Bridge.
I can assure the minister that I do not intend to take no for an answer on the question of the elimination of these roadside blights. Halfhearted landscaping consisting of the leveling of piles of rubble is as unacceptable as inaction. The Canadian public accepted the seaway as a national responsibility. Other Canadian organizations, both public and private, minute in comparison to the seaway, have accepted their responsibility for landscaping and frequently have allowed the use of such landscaped areas by the public. That the seaway authority, which possesses some of the most beautiful shoreline property in the Montreal region, should consider that its public responsibility consists solely in ensuring the unimpeded passage of ships in the seaway channel is to me a totally unacceptable proposition. Not only must the construction scars be eliminated, a promise now ten years unfulfilled, but landscaped parklands should take their place.
I appeal to the minister and to the seaway authority to fulfil this year the obligations of a term we hear frequently these days-good corporate citizenship. Surely the implications of this term to the seaway authority, a crown corporation, are of the utmost importance and weight.

I have been a passenger on several occasions when unusual things occurred. A few months ago the plane on which I was travelling was held in Val d'Or for the arrival of a patient from the hospital there. When the patient arrived we learned that a baby had been born prematurely some 20 minutes before the plane was due to leave. Since the nursing sisters did not have the necessary facilities to deal with the case in their hospital they had decided to use the air service knowing it would be a matter of minutes before the child could be taken care of in one of the large Montreal hospitals where all the necessary equipment was available. plane in the knowledge that within a short time they can be treated at one of the major hospitals.

abolishing the Royal Power of dissolution; institution of fixed dates of election, subject to power in the House of Commons itself to order an earlier date of election; abandonment of the constitutional convention whereby defeat of the Government in the House of Commons will normally result in a dissolution and the substitution therefor of a practice which would enable this House to determine in such event whether a government should continue in office, another government replace it or an election be held forthwith; provision that the House of Commons would have such continuity of existence that parliament might be summoned in event of an emergency arising during an election campaign; a requirement that financial provision for government be made before an election and the abandonment of the use of Governor General's warrants; changes in practice to enable the Commons more effectively to fulfil its traditional functions of making ministries responsible, initiating legislation, controlling supply and redressing grievances; and the adoption of other changes and reforms which will close the bewildering gap between the way in which parliamentary institutions and responsible government are supposed to work in theory and the way they do work in actuality.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last session I indicated that one of my personal centennial projects was to stimulate discussion and analysis in depth of the existing state of parliamentary institutions and responsible government. That is the object of this motion which obviously from its length is an omnibus one and virtually a speech in itself but which is modeled directly upon my private member's Bill No. C-61 now on the order paper. Bill C-61 spells out my current thinking and proposals in specific legislative form. There are members in this house who apparently have not read it.
In my view parliamentarians, political scientists, journalists, and indeed the public generally have become much too traditionalist and conventional in accepting the existing state of parliamentary institutions as the last word in democratic achievement. Most of the discussion about parliament relates to procedure, to rules, and to the standing orders. Almost none of the discussion affects the institutional aspects, the excellence of which seems to be taken for granted. If parliamentarians in the 1860's had been as self-satisfied about the excellence of governmental institutions as almost all their successors are today we should never have achieved confederation 100 years ago.
Suggested Committee on Procedural Changes
Canadians in the early days were the greatest political innovators of the democratic world. We were the real authors of the system of responsible government. We were the first to engraft a federal system of government upon the parliamentary system. Our originality in this respect has been admired and emulated in many parts of the world. Soon after confederation our political originality seems to have been stultified. Most parliamentarians and most political scientists accepted the responsibility of defending the status quo as the ultimate in political wisdom.
The last words of this motion state my opinion of the real problem. I believe that there has arisen, and I quote these words from the motion:
-a bewildering gap between the way in which parliamentary institutions and responsible government are supposed to work in theory and the way they do work in actuality.
Never have theory and practice been more widely separated. These words of the motion are based directly upon a comment by the leader of the House of Commons at Westminster, Richard Crossman, during a brilliant speech in that house on December 14, 1966. I quote from the British Hansard at page 482:
-there is one aspect of our institutions which is pernicious mumbo-jumbo. This is the wide and, to the ordinary elector, the baffling gap between the way in which our parliamentary system is supposed to work according to its procedures and the way it actually works in real life, between what we purport to be doing and what we actually do. It is this gap between parliamentary theory, parliamentary procedure, and parliamentary practice which, in my view, is largely responsible for the decline in the prestige of the House of Commons.
To that, Mr. Speaker, I say, amen.
This motion would provide the technique for the study in depth of that baffling gap. In my view there are three basic problems. First, the transfer of power from parliament to the executive has gone much too far. Second, so called responsible government has ceased in fact to be responsible and, third, independence in thought and action of the private members of parliament has been dangerously curtailed.
The late R. MacGregor Dawson put his finger directly on the problem, and I quote from the fourth edition of his "Government of Canada" at page 400:
Responsible government would appear to have suffered a strange and alarming inversion: the cabinet is no longer responsible to the Commons; the Commons seems instead to have become responsible to the cabinet.
That there is a substantial measure of truth in this, no one can deny.

Dick Crossman in his introduction to the latest edition of Bagehot sounds the same note on page 22 where he states:
Collective responsibility combined with the threat of dissolution have enabled the cabinet to become master of the assembly that created it.
To this truth we must add a further statement of Crossman at page 51 of his introduction:
The post-war epoch has seen the final transformation of cabinet government into prime ministerial government.
Instead of being what he once was, primus inter pares, the prime minister has achieved the position of grand vizier, never intended by the theorists or early practitioners of responsible government. I am not alone in so believing, and I quote from the Globe and Mail of January 10, 1967:
Opposition Leader John G. Diefenbaker says the office of prime minister of Canada has become allpowerful.
The article then states:
"The prime minister used to be regarded in the days of Macdonald as the first among equals," Mr. Diefenbaker said. "That no longer applies today. He's the first. There are no equals.
The prime minister in the days of Macdonald was not all-powerful. Today he is. When I say allpowerful, I refer to the period before an election. During an election, of course, democracy is restored."
That is a rather significant and discerning comment, and the inferences to be taken from it are rather considerable. The article then quotes the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert as follows:
"But between elections the power and authority of prime minister today is far beyond what it was in the days of Macdonald."
What I believe has happened is that we have engrafted much of presidential government upon the parliamentary system, without the checks and balances inherent at least in the United States system. Other factors involved in the shift in emphasis in power are the modern growth of the cult of personality, intensified by television, the hardening of party loyalties, the intensification of party discipline, the leader's control over the party machine, the virtual transfer of the power of dissolution into the hands of one man, the prime minister, and his use of the threat of dissolution as a disciplinary measure against ministerial and parliamentary colleagues alike, the rarity of resignation on questions of principle, the increasing percentage of parliamentarians of the majority party involved in some aspect of administration. Ministers of the crown have come to feel themselves the agents of the prime minister, owing allegiance to the man who gave them their job, rather than servants of the Commons. The most unfortunate by-product of this bewildering gap between theory and practice that I speak of in the last section of this motion has been the drastic curtailment of the independence of the private member. In my submission, what parliamentary institutions need more than anything else is a genuine restoration of the real independence of the peoples' representatives. The House of Commons needs to be made once again the real master of the administration. I believe we need to restore cabinet government as opposed to prime ministerial government and to make the cabinet actually responsible to the Commons, to correct what Dawson described as the "strange and alarming inversion."
With these objectives, the motion proposes that a special committee study a number of proposals listed in the motion. The first is the abolition of the royal power of dissolution. Let nobody be silly enough to continue the talk of the royal power of dissolution. It is not a royal power today; it is a prime ministerial power. I propose in substitution therefor the institution of a system of fixed dates of election subject, however, to a power in the House of Commons itself, not in the prime minister to order an earlier date of election.
The so-called royal power of dissolution, as I have said, has become in fact a prime ministerial power. Since 1926 the reserve of authority with the sovereign has virtually disappeared. There is no advantage in blinking this fact. Mr. St. Laurent, by devising in 1953 the technique of an instrument of advice for prime ministerial recommendations, effectively put the power of dissolution in the exclusive control of the prime minister acting alone and without the consent of his cabinet colleagues. Dissolution is one of the four things that a prime minister can recommend by instrument of advice without a minute of council, in which latter matters a quorum of cabinet must concur.

The power of dissolution is a carry-over from the days when the monarch was allpowerful and at will could send the people's representatives packing. Despite my good friend Dr. Eugene Forsey, who 1 think is one of our greatest Canadians and with whom I generally agree, the power of dissolution has become obsolete, has no inherent magic as a political instrument. Other reasonably enlightened nations manage to survive without it.
It has been argued in the press since my private member's bill was introduced that without this disciplinary power a prime minister would be powerless. I submit, sir, that this is a gross overstatement. Personally, I do not believe any one member of this House of Commons should have the exclusive right to terminate the life of this chamber. Equally, I do not believe that any one member, whether he be from Prince Albert or Algoma East, should have a disciplinary club to hold over independently-minded private members.
The concomitant, of course, of the abolition of dissolution must be the institution of fixed dates of election. Personally, I believe that if the life of this house were fixed we would have much less partisanship, at least for two or three years; we would be able to plan and execute our legislative and investigative program and do so in a much more efficient and expeditious manner. Would parliamentary stalemate be a possible result of fixed dates? I submit not. It is to avoid just such a possibility that I would propose a power in the House of Commons itself to fix an earlier election date. My proposals in this respect are set forth in detail in Bill C-61.
The next matter which the motion suggests for study by a special committee is the abandonment of the constitutional practice whereby defeat of a government proposal is considered defeat of the government and normally leads to an election. I propose the substitution therefor of a new constitutional practice which would enable this house itself, in such event, to decide whether the government should continue in office or be replaced by

On all government measures I believe the members of this house should have full independence of action without concern about the electoral consequences of defeating a government proposal. Each of us is sent here because our constituents have confidence in our judgment on public issues. But as soon as we arrive here, particularly when we are supporters of a government, we surrender our judgment to a system which makes mere voting robots of us.
It may be said that you cannot have 265 independent exercisers of judgment without chaos. I do not believe that. I have confidence in the general good sense of legislative bodies and confidence in my parliamentary colleagues. I think the people are entitled to expect and to receive the independence of judgment and action of each one of us. But so long as the present system continues the role of the private member supporting the government inevitably will be one of frustration and humiliation, a mere cog in a parliamentary machine designed for different and earlier days. I think we should ask ourselves, is it not possible that we can agree that the more leisurely days of Simon de Montfort or even those of Sir John A. Macdonald may have disappeared?
There are two other matters dealt with in this motion upon which I think there should be little basic disagreement. In my submission, sir, it is necessary by some technique or other, I care not what, to provide for continuity of existence of the House of Commons. In these days of rapidly developing crises both international and national the nation cannot afford to be without a legislative body for periods of 90 to 100 days. Yet that is what dissolution achieves. Dissolve parliament and the country becomes legislatively impotent for 30 days after an election, which election normally takes about 60 days. A parliament dissolved cannot be "undissolved". War, railway strike or any other emergency, with which only parliament can deal effectively, must await the return of the writs of election. How preposterous this is in this day and age.
The proposal I make in this motion is that each House of Commons have continuity of legal existence until its successors are elected, and thereby we would always have a legal, legislative authority to be summoned to deal with crises. Whether or not we adopt my suggestion of abolishing the power of dissolution, I submit that it must be changed or

Suggested Committee on Procedural Changes amended so as not to leave the nation legislatively powerless for periods which in today's rapidly moving world are relatively long.
I might point out by way of illustration that this appears to have been just the problem that deterred Mr. Mackenzie King, in view of the dangerous international situation in 1939, from advising a dissolution of parliament in the summer of that year. If he had done what he would like to have done, Canada would have been caught without a House of Commons at the outbreak of world war II. Would any Canadian feel confident if this parliament were in a state of dissolution at this particular time when conceivably we could be on the verge of another war of major proportions?

Four times in recent years parliament has been dissolved and there has been a massive resort to Governor General's warrants. After the dissolution in 1963 it fell to my lot, as the acting minister of finance, to sign the recommendations for Governor General's warrants and, sir, I say to you that no more distasteful duty ever came my way. I interject to say that the then minister of finance was wise enough to spend the whole election period in his own riding. As a result on election night I was left in a situation which I have since rectified.
In my submission these Governor General's warrants are an intolerable denial of the basic authority of the elected representatives. Question-Do you suggest moving toward a congressional system?
Answer-I used to take a dim view of the congressional as opposed to the parliamentary system. I still think our system has some basic advantages because, for one thing, it brings the executive into closer touch with the representatives of the people. But it also has some disadvantages, and I wouldn't be surprised if one day we find, as is so often the case, that the best solution would be the adoption of the best of both systems. This is the traditional Canadian approach to things-we take the best of the American and the best of the British and try to build up something Canadian. But I get very impatient these days when we spend hours in the House of Commons arguing whether one rule or another will be changed, whether we'll have ten men stand up instead of one man in order to block something. We have already made some very useful changes. But I would like to see a very thorough, non-partisan examination in depth of our parliamentary institutions.
So would I, Mr. Speaker. Whose words were those? They were the words of the right hon. member for Algoma East, the present Prime Minister of Canada. I am glad to read the integral text of this motion, because I now feel less alone in the House of Commons. Since my election to this

house, in all good faith, without fanaticism and in answer, I am sure, to a wish dear to the younger generation of Canadians that certain colonial traditions be put aside, I have always put on the order paper a resolution with that object in mind.
And now the hon. member of Carleton wishes to abolish the royal power of dissolution. This has made me feel that the house supports my objectives, which I would not call republican but which are the abolition of all symbols of colonialism and the proud affirmation of Canadian sovereignty, both symbolically and in practice.
However, before supporting the resolution of the hon. member for Carleton, it would be useful to know the concept or philosophy of the Conservative party as far as the royal prerogatives are concerned.
As recorded in Hansard of 1966 on page 4101, the Leader of the Opposition said the following:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point ol order in respect of the bill entitled "An act to amend the Criminal Code (repeal of power to commute a sentence of death)This bill should not be before parliament and it has no place on the order paper.
