Why did the Leader of the Opposition say such words? Because he thought that I wanted to abolish, by presenting this bill, a royal prerogative which consists in commuting to life imprisonment a death sentence. But, Mr. Speaker, is there a more important royal prerogative than the power of dissolution of the houses. Can there be a more important royal prerogative than this one: the dissolution of the houses; if the sovereign is to be made simply a symbol and if all his prerogatives are to be eliminated, it is necessarily a step towards the abolition of monarchy. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to get into the type of vindictive argument that appears to be developing as a result of the introduction of this motion. I believe that had the motion been introduced in a more conciliatory manner it would have received more support. Most people who have studied this motion and others like it, and who have listened to the proposals made by many persons will agree that there is a need for a conference to discuss in depth some of the changes which must be made in our system.
Part of this motion, which has been introduced now for four or five years, goes a long way in this direction. I refer to that section of the motion which deals with the power of the prime minister to call an election; and it is obvious that much abuse of this power has taken place during the last ten years.
Originally, Mr. Speaker, before the King-Byng issue, as pointed out by Dawson, the Governor General had considerable power.
DEBATES	693
Suggested Committee on Procedural Changes At that time I presume the royal prerogative, to which reference has been made this afternoon, was in fact in effect and that the Governor General of the day did have some power in the dissolution of parliament. Since I have been in parliament there have been a number of occasions when there was no justification whatever for the dissolution of parliament; it was merely a matter of the political advantage that could be gained by the prime minister of the day and his party.
This has meant, Mr. Speaker, five federal elections in eight years, and this as much as anything has brought the Canadian parliament into disrepute, not only in the eyes of Canadians but also those people in the newly emerging nations who are concerned with finding a model parliament with which to govern themselves.
This abuse has also led to a situation wherein, for many years now, there has been little constructive legislation which originated in parliament itself. In the main, legislation has been presented by the establishment and accepted by the cabinet. Cabinet ministers have had no time to concern themselves with the intricacies of their departments; they accept the point of view of the establishment simply because they are so busy conducting election campaigns that they are unable to get to know their own departments.
During the years I have been here, which include the four years when the Conservative government were in office, a continuous election campaign has been conducted because members knew that the minute the prime minister decided political advantage would be gained an election would be called. They were also aware of the fact that the Governor General perhaps did not have much knowledge of the parliamentary system or of his role in it, and he became a functionary willing to accept the dictates of the prime minister in this respect.
With regard to establishing a set term for parliament, I did suggest a four year period in a bill I introduced and which has been discussed several times. Some hon. members suggested that this was a republican idea and similar to the United States form of government. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we can accept a method that does seem to work in another country without changing our whole system.
It seems to me that the expression about throwing out the baby with the bath water has applicability to any type of parliamentary reform. In my opinion, I consider a four year
May 29, 1967
694	COMMONS
Suggested Committee on Procedural Changes term to be necessary in order to give members three years to conduct the legislative business of the country and a fourth year for campaigning purposes, instead of using all four years as at the moment simply because members do not know which year will be the last year of a parliament.
Obviously, with a four year term there would have to be some mechanism for deciding who would form the government if it were defeated. It is true that if the government were defeated in a major vote of nonconfidence, as distinct from the non-confidence motions we now move, the government would have to resign. The royal prerogative would come into effect and the Governor General would be in a position to call on somebody else to form a government. This would not be done on his own initiative, but after consultation with the leaders of all parties in the house. A substitute prime minister who would be acceptable to the other members of the house at the time would have to be found.
If, Mr. Speaker, the situation arose where a suitable prime minister could not be found, then a certain number of members-I suggested 15-would' move a motion of dissolution of parliament, and this would mean an election would be held. This motion would have to be supported by 75 per cent of the members of the house. I suggest 75 per cent because I think it would be foolish to suggest 51 per cent. With the lesser percentage the leader of the party would obviously say that if his members did not support his motion for dissolution he would not supply them with any election funds for the coming election. Therefore the majority would have to be considerably larger than just a mere margin.
If the situation arose wherein no government could stay in office and no party could form a government, there would have to be a safeguard to allow for dissolution of parliament when the members of parliament so decided. That is only natural.

The Financial Post put it succinctly on May 13 last when it stated:
Industry sources agree on one point-that expanding the Japanese market depends on a long term freight rate outlay not exceeding $4 per ton from the Coleman-Crowsnest pass area to tidewater.
The CPR's best offer to date is $4.60 per ton, and the producers are convinced the railway will not budge.
The producers contend that the $4 rate would be "more than generous", adding that its acceptance by the C.P.R. would enable them to greatly increase sales to Japan without federal subsidies.

business. Our trade with Japan is subsidized at the rate of $4 per ton. I should like to be fair with the present government and say that the subvention was put on by the Conservative government. Now I would like to say something a little more extensive about the Atlantic transportation studies. As all hon. members know, these grew directly out of the report of the Royal Commission on Transportation. The Mac-Pherson commission decided they could not take the time necessary to deal with particular problems in the Atlantic region and suggested that further investigation was required. That was the purpose of these studies.
The government, in preparing the national transportation bill, recognized that the Atlantic region presented particular problems which could not be dealt with without separate and detailed study of many aspects of transportation in the region, and the impact of transportation on the regional economy.
Discussions were held with the premiers of all four Atlantic provinces during 1965 to outline the purpose and scope of the study. A decision was made in the autumn of 1965 to commission consultants to carry out the required studies. The Department of Transport provided the funds and the study itself has been supervised jointly by officials of the

May 29, 1967
Supply-Transport
Atlantic Development Board and the Department of Transport.
The consultants were directed to assess the effectiveness of the existing transportation facilities and to determine the best means of developing these or alternative facilities to meet present needs and to foster the economic growth of the Atlantic provinces. The consultants were afforded complete freedom to carry out their investigations without official intervention of any kind. Their findings and conclusions were arrived at with a degree of independence as complete as that given to a royal commission.
The main study has been completed within the period of 18 months it was estimated would be required-I think they should be given full mai'ks for that-thanks to the cooperation afforded by provincial governments and the various community, business and transportation interests concerned.
The study is comprehensive and detailed and covers not only transportation in each individual province but also special research on various transportation services, such as the Newfoundland coastal services. Special studies were made of the possible effect on the Atlantic area of constructing a corridor road across the state of Maine between Quebec and New Brunswick, and of the problem of the seasonal fluctuation of the volume of traffic through the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
A particularly intensive study was made of the influence on the economies of the Atlantic provinces of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, the Freight Rates Reduction Act and the National Transportation Act.
While the conclusions of the consultants cover many aspects of transportation, they give particular emphasis to the need for further improvement and development of highways in the region and confirm the soundness of the federal support which has been given to the development of trunk roads in the Atlantic provinces since 1963. It will be recalled that the government made a decision in 1964 to give financial support to highway development in the north Gaspe area of the province of Quebec, rather than to extending the railway in that area.
When the main study was undertaken, it was recognized that if the study was to be completed within a reasonable period of time, certain additional studies might have to be carried out on a supplementary basis. As a result of the emphasis in the main study on the need to develop roads in the Atlantic

provinces, supplementary studies connected with trunk roads are now under way.
These studies are concerned with certain trunk roads in the province of Newfoundland, particularly in the Burin peninsula and on the northwest coast, and of the project for a highway across Labrador; with the development of the highway in New Brunswick from Moncton to the Quebec border via Bathurst and Campbellton; and with the development of the supplementary data relating to the roads in the Gaspe region, which is included in the area covered by the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
I mention these particular studies because there are a number of other roads which are dealt with in the main study, roads on Prince Edward Island, the road across the southern part of New Brunswick and a number of key trunk roads in Nova Scotia.
At its most recent meeting held in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, the Atlantic Development Board adopted a formal resolution recommending continued federal support for trunk roads in the Atlantic region to promote economic development.
I want to emphasize the next two paragraphs of this more or less written statement I am making now.
Conclusions reached by the consultants involve new approaches to transportation between the mainland and Newfoundland, particularly for services other than the present rail-ferry services. While these new conclusions will require careful examination, there is every intention on the part of the government to complete the work under way at the present and to improve railway terminal facilities at North Sydney and Port aux Basques.
In releasing these studies, it is the government's intention to provide all interested parties, whether public or private, with an opportunity to study and comment on their contents, and it is also the intention of the government to proceed expeditiously to examine the findings and conclusions with a view to formulating future policies.

The other day I collected, at random more or less, a list not only of the things which the government already had undertaken to do but also of the big transportation problems I could see ahead. It is really almost frightening when one realizes the amount that needs to be done

in this country if we are to have the kind of growth and development we want. In addition to the problems of the Atlantic region, there are a number of other major transportation problems which, because of their size and scope, fall outside the normal limits of present policy and require special attention. These include, for example, such items as the problem of an additional crossing of Vancouver harbour and the wider problem of the expansion of harbour developments at Vancouver; the question of an additional approach to Vancouver international airport on Sea island; road construction which may be required, in some cases, to offset railway branch line abandonments in the prairie provinces or elsewhere, and substantial additional expenditures and development which will be required if the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence seaway are to be expanded to meet the requirements of the future.
In addition there is the matter of improvement and possible deepening of the St. Lawrence ship channel below Montreal; major airport and air terminal expansion at Toronto and Montreal that will be necessary to take care of traffic requirements in the era of the jumbo jet and supersonic aircraft, as well as the question of better ground transportation arrangements to and from major metropolitan airports, and the possible need for harbour and railway expansion in the northern and northwestern areas of Canada to provide for economic exploitation of natural resources in those areas. Within the context of consideration of other urgent transport needs, the development of policy in all these fields becomes a matter of the greatest importance of the future of our country. I think perhaps at that point I might take my seat.

Mr. Speaker, last week I put a question to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) to determine to what extent the C.B.C. was disposed to make the necessary arrangements to promote French culture across the country, in short, to encourage the extension of the French fact from one ocean to the other.
According to statistics open to anyone, Canada has a population of 20 million people, 94 per cent of whom are reached by television.
After a thorough inquiry on broadcasting in Canada, the Fowler Commission said this:
-the C.B.C. is a vital factor of the Canadian radio-television system and the most important definite tool available for the development and maintenance of unity in Canada.
On page 37 of the same report, the following is stated:

We believe the C.B.C. has failed, and is failing today, to discharge adequately its duties to foster understanding between the two main cultural groups in this country. With rare exceptions, it does not produce programs that would assist English speaking Canadians to understand the attitudes and aspirations of French Canada. Equally the C.B.C. has failed to convey to French Canadians the doubts, uncertainties, ignorance, and good will of English Canadians concerning the "French Fact". The C.B.C. has itself made the following statement about its programming performance:
"The present schedules do not permit an adequate amount of intercommunication between French and English speaking Canadians; an adequate reflection of the diversified pattern of life, ideas and opinions from the various regions of Canada; an adequate development and utilization of Canadian writing and performing talents; or a proper diversification of foreign television entertainment."

Those are the words of the Fowler Commission which clearly show that the C.B.C. has not yet attempted to bring closer together the two main ethnic groups which make up Canada.
And to that end, I suggested to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) that

the C.B.C. could build-it would be a fine centennial project throughout the country relay stations which could retransmit French programs produced by the French network of the C.B.C. and enable several elements of our country to become acquainted with a culture that seems strange to them in some respects.
Canada has a population of 20 million people, 50 per cent of which is less than 26 years old. And because of a surprising broadmindedness shown by the younger generation its interest in strengthening Canadian unity, since the old fanaticisms are due to disappear, I think that it would be important for the French culture to span Canada from one ocean to the other at a cost that would probably be less to the government than that of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission, also responsible for promoting the French fact.
A repeater, as it is called, costs around $50,000. The operating cost is nominal. It would only be necessary to install repeaters in all the English-speaking capitals of the country, as well as in the main English-speaking centers which could precisely rebroadcast the French program of C.B.C. This would' permit the young people who learn French in school-somewhat as we have learned Latin when, after years of studies we are not even able to order a meal in Latin, just like in English schools where French is taught, when the time comes to turn to practice, to converse, practically nothing is remembered-to broaden their knowledge.
Therefore I make this suggestion to the Secretary of State to see what she thinks of it.

PUBLIC WORKS-HAZELTON, B.C.-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the community of Hazelton in British Columbia is the centre, perhaps by definition, of a rather goodly number of communities surrounding it. I am referring therefore to more than just the community of Hazelton itself. This area is in a very bad way economically. The base of the economy has been the logging and sawmill business. In recent times the bulk of the payroll in the area emanated from a fairly large sawmill. This sawmill has ceased operation, and in fact about the middle of the month, the 17th or 18th, and perhaps on both of these days, the capital assets of the company that were moveable were sold at auction. Those parts of the sawmill which were integral to its operation were moved out of the area. As a consequence, the one prospect that existed for the stability of the economy has now disappeared.
Many people, in anticipation of expanding activity, moved homes and families there. They are now faced with the prospect of
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion moving out again at the end of the school term. Those who are more tenacious are desirous of staying, in the hope that something additional will develop. The drain on social welfare payments will be increasing if a large number of people stay and if economic prospects do not improve.
As I understand the philosophy of the government, and I am not now desiring to argue about it, it is that of pump priming; that is, if public works can be used at a time of economic collapse or decline to stimulate the economy, even though it may only be for an interim period, then that is the sort of situation that should prevail. The minister's government has enunciated this thought on a number of occasions in the past.
Last year the estimates contained an amount of money for the construction of a federal building in the area. This project was cancelled because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) made a spurious bogey out of inflation. This proposed federal building disappeared from the estimates. As the matter stands now the building is scheduled, according to the latest information I have been able to obtain, not for this year's activity when it could be most helpful, but for the next fiscal year.
When we were dealing with the estimates of the Department of Transport, I raised the possibility of extending the Canadian National Railway from this point northward because that would be another stimulus to the economy of the area. I have been in communication with the Department of Industry and asked it to look at the situation to ascertain what could be done to promote industry to locate in the area. As we all know, this is a time consuming process and it may be many months before the Department of Industry accomplishes anything worth while, if in fact it is able to accomplish anything at all. There are local groups which have been in touch with industrial concerns in other parts of the nation, and indeed in the United States too. There are one or two prospects of economic activity there, but this is some time in the future.
I think that this is the ideal moment for the minister to put into effect his pump priming philosophy, as I have heard it called, in the Hazelton area, and make a start right away on this federal building. Even though the amount of money involved may be relatively small compared with other projects, nonetheless it will be helpful in an area which at the moment is in the doldrums economically

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable attention to what the hon. member has had to say. As I understand his argument, it is not that there is anything wrong with the plans of the department as such to proceed in the normal way, but rather that because of the special circumstances which have now arisen in this community owing to the shut down of the sawmill there the hon. member would wish the department to accelerate its planned program to put up this post office building. The hon. member would like the work commenced now because of the employment that it would provide. That seems to be the whole point of his argument.
If I have correctly summarized his point, may I say I will be very glad to look at this

matter. As he has indicated, no provision is made for this project in the estimates this year. There is of course the ever-pressing problem that seems to be constantly with us, that of finding the money to pay for these things. The taxpayers have to provide the money, and in the normal course this money would not be forthcoming for another year.
However, Mr. Speaker, in view of what the hon. member has said tonight I will re-examine the situation to see whether there is any reasonable prospect of expediting the matter and starting work right away, provided there are no other counterbalancing considerations which would take precedence. In any event, I will undertake to make a thorough examination of the matter in the light of what he has said tonight, and that I will make an announcement in due course.

subtopic: SUMMARY OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION AND THE U.S.S.R. COUNCIL OF MINISTERS COMMITTEE FOR RADIO AND TV BROADCASTING

speechtext: The C.B.C. has entered into agreement with the broadcasting organization in the U.S.S.R. -the U.S.S.R. council of ministers committee for radio and T.V. broadcasting-under terms which can be summarized as follows.

Under terms of the agreement, concluded on April 26, 1967, both parties will exchange radio and television programs of interest to Canadian and Soviet listeners. The radio program exchange will include selected literary, scientific-educational items, sport and children's programs, as well as taped recordings of classical, folk and modern music, operas and concerts. The television exchange will include short film features depicting happenings in both countries, as well as musical, sport, documentary and children's items.
Under the agreement, both parties will attempt to establish an exchange of staff with the sender meeting travelling expenses and the recipient covering living expenses within the country. The exchange of radio and T.V. programs will be conducted on a no-charge as well as on a commercial basis. Purchase and sale of T.V. material and films, as well as of musical recordings and other radio and T.V. programs, will be conducted by both parties on the basis of further agreements. Those exchanged on a no-charge basis will be used by each party at its own discretion. However, these programs will not be made available to a third party and will not be used for commercial purposes. Changes and/or cuts in programs are not to distort their content.

maintopic: DOCUMENTARY PRODUCTION IN THE SOVIET UNION

speechtext:
(a) General:
A supplementary agreement to the above allows the C.B.C. to make television documentary films in the U.S.S.R. Both parties can take the initiative in proposing subjects for filming and the subject area and scenario plans of a film must be jointly agreed upon.
Particular attention will be given to topics promoting Canadian-Soviet relations. The C.B.C. has agreed to give consideration to the recommendations, comment and proposals of representatives of the Soviet committee regarding content of these films in the interest of making accurate and objective films about the U.S.S.R. and its people.
(b)	Composition of Crews:
The Soviet committee will facilitate the entry into the U.S.S.R. and the participation in the filming, of a complete C.B.C. camera crew, producer and reporter, except in cases where the C.B.C. chooses to provide less than a full crew. The duration of the filming will be agreed upon in advance and will be based on shot lists proposed by the C.B.C.
(c)	Processing:
Soviet radio and T.V. guarantees the processing in the U.S.S.R. of exposed film. The C.B.C. reserves the right to negotiate on the processing in Canada of exposed film whenever technical reasons appear to make this desirable.
(d)	Broadcasting of Programs:
(i)	In Canada
When the work on the film in Canada has
been completed, the C.B.C. will send the final version of the film to Moscow for viewing by authorized officials of the Soviet committee. The purpose of such viewing is to permit the committee to see the final version of the film produced by the C.B.C. and to comment upon it. Under the agreement, there is no power of veto. However, before broadcasting the final version, the C.B.C. has agreed to take into full consideration the Soviet comments.
(ii)	Abroad
Approval of both parties is required for distribution outside Canada.
(e)	Financial Conditions:
Financial conditions involved in filming and distribution are to be the subject of separate negotiation and agreement.
Tuesday, May 30, 1967
